scenes.title: The Variable Definition File
scenes.narration: Lab 18's variables all had defaults. But production configurations usually refuse to guess: variables declared with no default must be supplied — and the standard supplier is a file. This lesson is terraform dot t f vars, the definition file Terraform loads automatically.

scenes.heading: What you'll learn
points: Variables without defaults are required — Terraform prompts or errors
terraform.tfvars is auto-loaded by name on every plan/apply
-var-file selects alternate files (prod.tfvars, staging.tfvars)
One declaration, many value files — environments without copies

Three: var dash file selects alternate files — prod, staging. Four: one declaration, many value files — environments without copies.

scenes.narration: This is lab nineteen. Last lesson made the inputs strict — validation rejecting bad values. Today's question: where do good values come from? Terraform's answer is a file it loads by convention, plus a flag for everything else.

scenes.heading: Auto-loading by name
points: terraform.tfvars (and terraform.tfvars.json) loads automatically
*.auto.tfvars loads too — ordered by filename
-var-file=prod.tfvars adds any file, on demand
No default + no value = Terraform prompts interactively (or errors in CI)
scenes.narration: The convention is the feature. Name the file terraform dot t f vars, and Terraform loads it on every plan and apply — no flags, no scripts. Any file ending in dot auto dot t f vars loads too. Need a different environment? Keep a prod t f vars and pass var dash file. And if a required variable has no value anywhere, Terraform stops and asks. The declaration stays in code; the values stay in data.

scenes.narration: As always, the lab is in the course GitHub repository under Section 1, Foundations, with the link in the description. Main dot t f declares three variables with no defaults — and terraform dot t f vars is where the values live.

Three variables, and notice what's missing: no type keyword beyond the bare minimum, and no defaults anywhere. Location, name prefix, tier — declared and required. Terraform will not invent values for these. The configuration refuses to run until someone supplies them.

The consumption is familiar from lab eighteen: the storage account's name assembles the prefix with a random suffix, and the tier flows straight from the variable. The only difference is upstream — nothing here has a fallback. Every value in this block came from outside.

And here's the outside: terraform dot t f vars. Three assignments — one per variable, matching names exactly. No flags needed: Terraform loads this file by name, automatically, on every run. Rename it and it stops loading — the name is the contract.

scenes.caption: The definition file feeds the run
scenes.narration: The data flow, drawn out: the definition file is picked up by name, its values land in the required variables, and the resources consume them — no defaults involved anywhere.

steps.narration: Terraform dot t f vars is auto-loaded by name on every run.
Its values land in the three required variables — location, name prefix, tier.
And they flow straight into the build: the region to the group, the prefix and tier to the storage account.
Code declares; data supplies. Swap the file, and the same code builds a different environment.

scenes.narration: Two runs, one configuration. The apply picked up terraform dot t f vars automatically — no flags at all. Then the same code with a different file: var dash file, prod t f vars, and the plan targets a different region, a different prefix, a different tier. Nothing edited. Environments are files, not copies of the code.

scenes.heading: Common pitfall — mistaking the example file for the real one
points: Only terraform.tfvars auto-loads — terraform.tfvars.example does not
No default + missing value = an interactive prompt (or a hard error in CI)
-var-file can be passed multiple times — later files win
Values on the command line (-var) beat every file
scenes.narration: Here are the pitfalls in this lab. One: only terraform dot t f vars auto-loads — the example file does not. The dot example suffix means Terraform ignores it completely; copy it, rename it, and fill it in. Two: no default and a missing value means an interactive prompt — or a hard error in c i. In c i there's no one to answer the prompt, so the missing variable stops the run — which is exactly why the file convention matters. Three: a var file flag can be passed multiple times — later files win. That lets you layer a base file with an environment override. Four: values on the command line beat every file. The var flag has the highest precedence of all.

points: No default = required variable — Terraform prompts or errors
terraform.tfvars auto-loads by name on every plan/apply
-var-file swaps in environment files (prod.tfvars)
Precedence: -var beats -var-file beats auto-loaded files
Code declares; data supplies — environments are files, not copies
scenes.narration: Quick recap — five things. One: no default means a required variable — Terraform prompts, or errors. Two: terraform dot t f vars auto-loads by name on every plan and apply. Three: the var file flag swaps in environment files, like prod dot t f vars. Four: precedence — a var flag beats a var file, which beats auto-loaded files. Five: code declares, data supplies — environments are files, not copies.
Now that we understand how this Terraform configuration works, in the next part of this video, we'll move to a real-world demo and deploy it in Microsoft Azure.
